[WP] "I awoke to find a mysterious figure digging me from my grave."

"What the hell took you so long?" The words sputtered in rasping cadence. The figure seemed short and wiry for someone who dug so quickly. James threw his hands up over the edge of his grave, twisting the damp grass in his fingers. The dim glow of the lantern resting at the feet of his savior was a tiny sun, but dancing lights were a fair price to look upon the small graveyard in which he came to rest. He recognized it, a cemetery just past the hardware store, its beech trees always shaking under the breath of a mysterious breeze.

The cloaked figure jammed its shovel into a pile of reddish earth and knelt beside James, wrapping a gloved hand around his wrist. The tug was enough to pull him effortlessly above ground, but unprepared, James splayed out with a dull thud.

He coughed, washing the taste of iron over his tongue, playing back a faint memory of his first school brawl.

"You're a strong ox, aren't you? Who hired you to come get me? Lemmy maybe, old bastard knew I was here; or Tasha, she always loved me to much to believe I'd croak so easy. C'mon, out with it."

The figure raised an arm to brush some dirt from James's shoulder, and a thick clacking echoed between them. It turned away, seemingly staring at the wisps of clouds encircling the moon and wrung its hands. James felt something scurry up his leg, but as he smashed his palm against it, nothing was there. Shifting his gaze, the figure had started lurching toward the large steel gates, swinging loosely in the moonlight.

"Right." Unease crept into the base of James's skull, rattling loose a twinge of fear. It made him focus, pulling all of his senses into learning all about the cloaked figure. It was abnormally short and wide, each step jiggling its frame underneath the cloak. The cloak itself was a patchwork mess of different cloth, tailored suit here and rags somewhere else. Aside from the occasional clacking, it made no noise while they walked toward the gate.

"So where are we going?" Another slew of clacking as it pressed the gate open for James to slip through. The figure let the gate slide shut, again wringing its hands. James turned to catch a glimpse under its hood while the moon slipped from behind the clouds; he managed to make out a jaw-line, grizzled with a beard. It shook as the figure turned back to the cemetery, and James heard the clatter of something hitting the ground. The moon was gone though, obscuring whatever lay just beyond reach.

"So, I guess we're done then?" A final clacking from the figure made James's skin crawl.

"Fine, I'll just leave you to your work." He turned and started down the path toward town. With each step, the soreness from lying in the casket weighed upon him. Even breathing took its toll, kicking up blood from his parched throat. At some point, his vision began to blur. His gate slowed to a crawl, and finally, under a dying beech tree, he sat to take a rest.

James eyes shot open, and he frantically looked out into the darkness. It felt like he'd slept for a long time, but it was still night. At some point, he must have laid down, but grass shouldn't be this soft. A light scratching noise echoed around him, as though a dog was pawing to be let in. Reaching out, his hand quickly grazed against a thin veil of silk covering a hard surface. Panic flooded in, followed by screams. They drowned out everything-- except for the memories flooding back in. Lemmy and Tasha laughing as James heard the dirt piling up. Their curses and slurs for him. His eyes itched. Screams turned to threats, and finally to begging. His eyes itched. The darkness of the casket made the world endless--a lie just like his life. James heard something moving--clacking--with him in the casket.

His eyes itched.

The last time I made a post like this, I wrote about Pool of Radiance, and it's emphasis on non-combat sources of experience, but also engaging tactical combat.

Today I want to talk about the very first Wizardry. This came out in 1981, and I strongly recommend this amazing series of articles about the history and making of Wizardry. It starts at a castle on the border with Nazi Germany. And if that doesn't hook you, I don't know what will.

There were honestly not many RPGs of note before Wizardry even came out. A few experimental mainframe games, and the first Ultima or two, if you count Akalabeth. But even the first Ultima games treated the RPG aspect so bizarrely. Their mechanics more closely resembled Gauntlet where you just walk into enemies until they are dead, and purchase an uncapped amount of health or stats to "level up". Wizardry more closely pulled from Dungeons & Dragons, using it's basic classes, it's dual classing concept, even using their notion of armor class starting at 10 and working downwards. But the biggest thing Wizardry brought to CRPGs was party based combat, a static dungeon design, and rudimentary puzzles. Also you had to draw maps, on paper. I love it.

And despite being called a "Sad game for sad people" by this guy Wizardry holds up remarkably well today. It's really fast, gives you a good sense progression, and the dungeon feels genuinely threatening, but with ample secrets to discover. The first 4 levels are especially good, but it begins to feel like more of a grind after that. Once again, it uses a very similar magic system to D&D where your spells are bracketed into levels, and you can only cast so many spells of each level per trip into the dungeon. Spells are your primary resource to manage, and in many ways your only resource. Money becomes rather inconsequential before long. But you will always be sweating how many spells you still have available, and whether you've been pushed to the point where you need to bail yet.

However, not all is roses and rainbows. Wizardry is not just hard, but frequently bullshit. It has permadeath. You characters can die of old age, although this is unlikely. What is likely to happen is for a revive spell to fail, turning your poor dead party member to ash. Then you need to cast a rebirth spell, which also has a chance to fail. If that fails, then the character is just as gone as if he died of old age. What severely aggrevates the permadeath is that many enemies have a decapitation ability. Vorpal Bunnies are the first you'll run into, followed by Ninjas. Ninjas especially will ambush you on the 3rd level, and might decapitate a character before you even get a chance to act! The emphasize how ruinous this can be, I need to point out one last fact. The game is constantly saving. Ironman mode is the only mode. No take backs.

But that is not to say that Wizardry is not rewarding, and that there is nothing you can do. Playing the Apple II or Commodore 64 versions, you are best off making backups of your scenario disk. I'm under the impression this was a common practice even back in the day when these games came out. But Wizardry was one of the first games I know of to have a cheat program sold by a 3rd party! It was such a problem that Sirtech began packing a warning in with the game that use of a 3rd party cheat program would void your warrantee. Because back then the disc would wear out with repeated play. Today you can just use a hex editor if your party of adventures gets ambushed by ninjas and every single member gets decapitated 30 seconds into your play session. The character format is very well understood.

I would strongly caution people away from the DOS version. Rumors are abound that the random number generator is just borked in that version, or that for whatever perverse reason they've just made the game harder. The known statistics involved in Wizardry are best summarized here, and speaking from my own personal experience, the DOS version does not reflect this at all. Most blatantly, there is a supposed to be a 50% chance to revive a dead character, plus 3 times their vitality. I never successfully revived anyone across a dozen attempts in the DOS version. Other oddities include there supposedly being a 85% chance for a character's statistics to improve when they level. However my experience in the DOS version is that may barely break even, and mostly go down. I also have serious suspicions about the RNG where it relates to how often status effects like decapitation, poison and paralysis kick in.

So what version should you play? The Apple II Disc 1 Disc 2 and Commodore 64 versions are freely available and the emulators A2 C64 for these systems are well developed. However, the UIs for these games is a significant step backwards from the DOS version which featured many graphical and UI upgrades. The version most people seem to swear by is the Japanese SNES version, which has vastly improved graphics, a good UI, and some gameplay enhancements for the Theif class. It also has some rudimentary English options. But there is also a full English romhack available quite easily. Regardless of which version you choose, my experience in all of them has felt much more balanced and fair compared with the DOS version. My characters have actually improved with each level, I've successfully revived dead characters, and I think the Ninjas decapitate people at a more reasonable rate than nearly 100%.

Regardless of which version of Wizardry you play, or how far you make it before you ragequit, it's definitely interesting to see how many of it's influence persist today.

Can confirm: Made multiple backups of scenario disks and used the backups to play. Copy2+ baby!! It was still a pain in the ass when you needed to reload. The Apple2e had such small memory (64k) you had to keep swapping out disks during a copy. I had the 80 column card that doubled the ram but using it was very situational. Dual disks were a nice thing to have but were pricey!! My dad would always point out that the machine had cost more than the car he drove to work when it was new.

Wizardry and Ultima were both awesome!! Groundbreaking. Everyone agreed... but I need to clarify "everyone." I had a graduating class of close to 800 and there were maybe 3 or 4 people with an Apple. Maybe 10 with a computer at home. All of the student owned machines were far advanced compared to the card reading Wang in the computer class room. FUCK that WANG!! Goddammit.... still pissed off at that POS and at having to fill in scantron cards and at not being allowed to touch the keyboard! (calming down.. gotta let it go... been almost 30 years since I left that soul crushing, windowless hell-hole of a prison.) Anywho, my point being that there were very few of us playing these games. Almost everything was word of mouth. We photo copied each others maps... and after a certain level the maps were important. You could memorize the first few levels but then you would reach a point where the floor would spin or teleport you... with little if any visual indications.

I can still remember typing in spell names frantically... Tiltowait? Zilwan?

Anyway.. thanks OP for stirring up the memories.. good and bad. Now I have to drag the old girl out and fire her up again. She still ran as of 2010 and the old elephant disks still read.
So now that I've lured in an actual Wizardry Veteran, I have to ask, how many times did you party wipe and what did you do? I'm curious how many rage quits this game inspired in its day.

Well, that's a bit complicated. The short answer is countless rage quits. Only that term had to wait decades to come into existence.

The long answer....

Disks were not cheap. A couple of bucks a week allowance does not put a dent in a box of floppys. When I did finally get a job the minimum wage was $3.25. So, you buy the cheap ones. Cheap disks had failed the QA test on one side and were put in a single sided sleeve. You then took a hole punch and notched the disk so you could write on both sides. Not too shabby when you consider it doubled your KB for the money. The point of this was that that disk was going to fail. Not "If." Just "When." I still have nightmares of the sound of the head resetting. Goto 2:00 on this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eZiLEp3zv_0) for the sound. (I still cringe.) So if you were smart, you used a good disk for your character disks. And you always ran off the copy. It was common for the game company to have supplied the program on one disk that was read only (no notches) and a character disk that was writable. Elephant double sided, double density disks were the best IMHO. Their catch phrase was “Elephants Never Forget.” I don’t know about “never” but I can attest to 30ish years. Failure to use a good disk meant you would eventually nuke the disk and have to spend hours using the aforementioned CopyII+ to read a single sector over and over and over, hoping you would get a good read.. often times you were just fucked.. And don’t even get me started on how common household magnets were back in the day... get one within a couple feet of your collection and you would be crying for weeks. So permadeath was much less of a threat than disk failure. Difficulty levels were uncommon and we just wanted to see what was around the next corner more than we wanted bragging rights. We could and did plug the video output to a VCR and record some things but just being able to say: “I got the gems in and took the shuttle to the wizard's castle and beat his ass and then grabbed the burning crystal” was usually enough bonafides to get a head nod and a seat at the table. From there it would take a couple of conversations to determine if you had the prerequisite knowledge to hang with the geeks... If you had this knowledge it was assumed you had figured it out yourself or with the help of a few other nerds because the documentation for all of this was pretty much nonexistent. This was important as I will explain in a sec.

Games were not common. And there was no gaming store for computers (eventually the board game & toy stores carried Atari cartridges but that was later.) No magazines dedicated to gaming and very few sources of info on a title. Hell, the only kind of stores that had any computer magazines also had adult magazines (no porn on VCR yet) and as a kid you weren't allowed in those stores (18+ with an ID.) The computer store was the closest thing we had and there were maybe 3 titles on that shelf at any given time... they only got in a few copies of each and the employees bought those right away. SO, you did the only sensible thing. You made friends (or at least respectful acquaintances) and copied the shit out of anything you could. We were still years away from any type of laws that made this illegal. It took the VCR becoming mainstream that for those laws to get bought and passed. Several times I bundled all my floppies into my luggage and flew 1200 miles across the country to trade with my cousins and return with maybe 10-20 games. But half of what you got on any given run were either complete crap (the copy session was the 1st time you heard of a title) or the disks did not survive the trip copy correctly in the 1st place. So this whittled it down to a few with actual replay value and nothing with dynamic levels (until Activision's Pitfallon Atari.) You played those and beat them for the 80th time and eventually found your way back to Wizardry which was nearly impossible to beat and required a LOT of patience. Considering the near absolute lack of any type of entertainment for geeks we had a lot of time on our hands though..

Lot of water under the bridge. I would be happy to answer any questions.... even if you just want to hear about the mastodon hunts or the day we 1st made fire..
